question: Which mechanism is responsible for the terbinafine resistance observed in the current Indian epidemic of chronic dermatophytosis?

answers.text: Point mutations in the squalene epoxidase (SQLE) gene that reduce terbinafine binding to its target enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase in the ergosterol synthesis pathway. Mutations in the SQLE gene — well documented in the Trichophyton mentagrophytes/indotineae complex prevalent in India — reduce drug-target binding, producing clinical resistance and driving the switch to itraconazole for recalcitrant disease.

answers.text: Mutations in the lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51) gene that reduce drug binding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CYP51 mutations affect azole antifungals (itraconazole, fluconazole), not terbinafine. Terbinafine acts upstream in the ergosterol pathway at squalene epoxidase, and it is mutations at this enzyme that drive terbinafine resistance.

answers.text: Acquired loss of the fungal chitin cell wall, preventing drug entry

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fungi do not lose their chitin cell wall — it is essential for structural integrity and survival. Terbinafine resistance is a target-enzyme mutation (squalene epoxidase), not a cell wall alteration.

answers.text: Overproduction of ergosterol stimulated by topical antibacterial agents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While topical steroid misuse contributes to treatment failure through immunosuppression and spread, the specific drug resistance is due to genetic mutations in the squalene epoxidase enzyme, not antibacterial-driven ergosterol overproduction.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key mechanism is a point mutation in the squalene epoxidase gene — terbinafine's molecular target — not a change in cell wall or a different enzyme.
SQLE mutations explain why itraconazole — which acts on a different enzyme (CYP51) — has become the rescue agent for terbinafine-resistant tinea.
